title: Cobweb load scribble — elastic prefetch and jitter runs
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad of the last week of runs: trying an "elastic prefetch" (client-side micro-delay that coalesces very short back-to-back requests) + server KV-cache warmness tuning on a small, heterogeneous dev fleet. Goal: reduce p99 tail amplification during mixed-size arrivals while keeping p50 stable and not inflating cost by adding idle batching.

Setup summary (dev cluster):
- 8-node dev fleet: 3xA100-80GB, 3xA10, 2xT4 (intended to emulate mixed prod).
- Runtime build: local branch elastic-prefetch-v3 (see PR above).
- Model: open-gpt-2-medium-quant (tokenization ~ 1.1 tokens/byte), sequence length sampled from empirical distribution from the last 7d prod trace (median 64, heavy tail to 1024).
- Client generator: hybrid driver (poisson baseline lambda + periodic microbursts every 45s, duration 3-9s, amplitude 1.5–3x).
- Workload split: 70% short (<=64), 20% mid (65–256), 10% long (>256).
- KV-cache: baseline TTL=3s (old); tuned to 6s and 12s for experiments; cache is per-model, per-tenant variant.
- Batch policy: continuous batching enabled, max batch size = 64 tokens, batch timeout = 20ms default unless overwritten by policy.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
1) baseline (no prefetch, TTL=3s)
2) TTL=6s
3) TTL=12s
4) client elastic-prefetch enabled (micro-delay 8–12ms distribution) + TTL=6s
5) elastic-prefetch + TTL=12s + slightly raised batch timeout (30ms)

Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies (in ms), end-to-end (client observed), server queue wait, GPU utilization, KV-cache hit rate, token cost estimate (tokens x cost factor). Sample window length: 20 minutes per run, repeated 3x per config at different random seeds.

Representative results (median over repeats):
- Baseline (TTL3): p50=42ms, p90=110ms, p95=210ms, p99=980ms, kv-hit=18%, gpu-util avg=72%
- TTL6: p50=44ms, p90=108ms, p95=190ms, p99=860ms, kv-hit=27%, gpu-util avg=75%
- TTL12: p50=45ms, p90=105ms, p95=180ms, p99=700ms, kv-hit=34%, gpu-util avg=76%
- Prefetch+TTL6: p50=48ms, p90=95ms, p95=140ms, p99=260ms, kv-hit=39%, gpu-util avg=78%
- Prefetch+TTL12+30ms: p50=50ms, p90=92ms, p95=130ms, p99=210ms, kv-hit=44%, gpu-util avg=79%

Interpretation / quick notes:
- Increasing KV TTL progressively reduces p99 but has diminishing returns beyond 12s on this dev fleet. The effect is more pronounced for heavy-tail (>256) requests because they benefit from cached prefixes.
- Client-side elastic-prefetch dramatically reduces p99 (980->260ms) while modestly shifting p50 (42->48ms). That tradeoff is promising: small, controlled delays allow natural coalescing without adding large batching timeouts.
- Raising the batch timeout to 30ms only added ~2–3ms to p50 compared to prefetch alone yet trimmed p99 further (260->210ms) — likely because longer micro-window captured extra short inter-arrivals.
- GPU utilization increased slightly (72->79%) when combining prefetch+cache, which aligns with more effective token packing and lower per-token overheads. This implies lower per-token cost even if wall-time per-request increases a touch for short requests.

Observed pathological cases:
- During periodic microbursts, nodes with slower GPU (T4) showed transient queue buildup; p99 there spiked to ~900ms in baseline. With TTL12+prefetch the spike was limited to ~280ms.
- A misconfigured client seed (one run) set micro-delay to 40ms accidentally and produced worse p50/p90 (p50 up to 120ms); this confirms sensitivity to the delay parameter. Keep default 8–12ms range.
- Long sequence requests (>512) still dominate tail beyond p99. Prefetch helps by improving prefix cache for reused contexts, but cannot avoid raw compute time for long sequences. Consider explicit long-request routing to dedicated capacity for strict SLOs.

Profiler snapshots (annotated):
- When p99 climbs above 600ms, server-side breakdown shows: 60% queue wait, 30% GPU compute, 10% serialization/transfer. With prefetch+TTL12, queue wait reduces to 15% of end-to-end.

Quick checklist for next actions:
- [ ] Run same matrix on stable dedicated pool (no T4s) to confirm that heterogeneity is the main amplifier for tails.
- [ ] Add a control that routes long (>512) to a dedicated lane and measure end-to-end SLO improvement and cost delta.
- [ ] Instrument finer-grained client-side telemetry to confirm that prefetch actually groups requests from same client vs different clients (I suspect both).
- [ ] Validate behavior with production-like token distributions (higher long-request fraction).
- [ ] Add small A/B in-host test comparing prefetch distribution 6–10ms vs 12–18ms to confirm optimum.

Implementation notes / gotchas to remember:
- Prefetch/micro-delay must be randomized per request to avoid sync alignment across clients. Use triangular distribution center=10ms, min=5ms, max=15ms for production experiments.
- When increasing TTL, ensure memory pressure on KV store is monitored; 12s on dev was safe but scale could push memory bounds. Add eviction logging.
- Ensure cache keys are normalized by model-variant and tenant; accidental mismatch found in one run (lowered hit rate).

Short-term conclusion:
Elastic client prefetch + modestly longer KV TTLs looks like a low-risk, high-reward knob to reduce p99 tail amplification on mixed-size workloads. It trades a couple ms at p50 for dramatic p99 improvements and better GPU packing. Next step: verify on a more production-like fleet and add long-request routing experiment.

Notes to self: leave runtime flag gated and default off for customers, opt-in via feature flag for early testers. Add telemetry for "prefetch_coalesced" boolean on traces.

Raw experiment IDs (for traceability):
- run-20250214-cwb-01
- run-20250216-cwb-03
- run-20250217-cwb-07

End of scribble.
